newsitem.title: USA: Delay in Big Dig financing could cost Mass. $1 bln.
newsitem.headline: Delay in Big Dig financing could cost Mass. $1 bln.

text.p: The Massachusetts Legislature has until the end of March to approve Gov. William Weld's $4.3 billion transportation issue or the nation's largest construction project could cost taxpayers another $1 billion.

Gov. Weld's $4.3 billion bond to fund all state transportation projects through 1999, allocated $3.1 billion to the Third Harbor/Central Artery project, also known as the Big Dig, and $1.2 billion for the rest of the state's bridges and roads program.
The artery portion qualifies the state for federal funds for the $10.7 billion projects next two years.

But lawmakers and the administration must approve both the bond and the new Big Dig financing plan -- the Metropolitan Highway System -- by an April 1 deadline imposed by the Federal Highway Administration.
This is the first time that the FHA has required a detailed financing plan to be in place for the nation's largest public works project.

Controversy has surrounded a $1.5 billion portion of the bond that the state intends to secure with Grant Anticipation Notes or GANs that will allow Massachusetts to borrow money based on FHA grants it expects to receive in 2002 and beyond.
"If we use traditional funding it could stretch this out 10 years and add $1 billion" to the project, Massachusetts Turnpike chief financial officer James Rooney told a legislative panel.
But state legislators are worried that Washington, now in the process of reformulating how federal transportation funds are apportioned, will send Massachusetts far less than the GANs assume.
The Massachusetts Taxpayers Foundation, a good government group, warned in a report released last week that the state is likely to come up $570 million short in the Big Dig financing as now proposed.
